messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Maria is a 55-year-old Latina woman who works as a bank teller in a small suburban branch. She is divorced and lives alone. She came to therapy at the urging of her supervisor, who noticed she had become increasingly jumpy around customers, especially when someone dropped a heavy coin tray or when a car backfired outside the drive-through lane. Maria agreed to talk because she was exhausted—exhausted from watching every face that approached her window, from flinching at every unexpected noise, and from the hollow feeling that had settled into her chest years ago and never left.

The event that changed everything happened over twenty years ago, during her deployment as a U.S. Army medic in Iraq. She was part of a medical convoy moving through a rural area when an IED detonated under the vehicle in front of hers. The explosion was a deafening, concussive bang that seemed to come from everywhere at once. Her Humvee stopped, and she ran forward with her kit. The soldier she reached first—a young man named Rivera, with whom she had shared jokes just that morning—was already gone. She remembered the feel of his uniform under her hands, the coarse, sand-gritted fabric wet with blood, and the way his face was slack and wrong. She tried to work on him anyway, but it was futile. The scene around her was chaos: shouts, smoke, the metallic smell of blood and burned rubber. She could never later put the sequence of those minutes into the right order. When she tried to tell her family after she came home, she would start, then lose the thread, then stop altogether. The memory felt like something that could not have actually happened to her—so extreme, so far from the ordinary life she had known, that she sometimes wondered if she had dreamed it.

In the years that followed, Maria’s life narrowed. She married and divorced, and the marriage failed in part because she could not explain why she would freeze when her husband put on a certain jacket with a rough, sandpapery texture, or why she would not go to Fourth of July celebrations. She learned to avoid conversations about loss. When a coworker talked about a relative who had died, Maria felt her throat tighten and her hands begin to tremble, so she politely excused herself. She came to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous—that danger could come from anywhere, at any second, and she had to be ready. At the bank, she found herself scanning customers as they entered: their posture, their eyes, the way they held their hands. She studied faces for signs of threat, reading body language the way she used to read a patient’s vitals. When a customer sighed heavily or shifted weight, her heart would pound and her stomach would clench. She had physical reactions to reminders she did not even consciously identify: a particular synthetic fabric on a child’s backpack, the sound of a car door slamming too hard. She knew, on some level, that she was not in a war zone anymore, but her body did not believe it.

Nothing in her life felt meaningful now. She went to work, came home, watched television, slept fitfully. She had stopped seeing friends because she could not stand the effort of pretending she was fine. The thing that finally drove her to call a therapist was an incident last week. A customer came to her window and began telling a story about losing his wife to cancer. Maria felt a surge of heat, her vision went spotty, and she had to ask another teller to take over. She went to the break room and sat shaking, and she realized she could not keep living this way—half in the present, half in an explosion that had happened two decades ago. She is terrified that she is broken beyond repair, but she also harbors a small hope that maybe there is a way to make the memory feel real and to let herself be safe again.
